source.title: Robust Predictive Uncertainty and Double Descent in Contaminated Bayesian Random Features
source.authors: Michele Caprio; Katerina Papagiannouli; Siu Lun Chau; S. Mukherjee

record.tranche_reason: Tests double descent in random-feature regression, a model setting distinct from the deep-network settings in the claim, including under label contamination.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own random-feature test-error sweeps and predictive-variance envelopes. Results cited from other work are not recorded as rows. The plotted values are not tabulated, so figure-only results are recorded without estimating numbers from the plots.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own simulations of random-feature regression. It sweeps N/d and reports test-error double descent with a peak near N = n, a bias-variance decomposition showing the peak is variance-driven, and peak height growing with the label-outlier fraction. Its main contribution is theoretical: contamination bounds on predictive variance. The peak-preservation results are derived by construction from the baseline variance.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct, but it should lead with the theoretical result. Contamination bounds act as affine or positive rescalings of the classical Bayesian random-feature predictive variance. Under the assumption that the baseline variance shows double descent, these bounds preserve the peak location. The simulations show a variance-driven peak, and a peak amplified by label outliers without shifting. The authors stress that the method aims at robust uncertainty quantification, not better test error.
record.recipe_differences: Uses Bayesian random-feature regression, contamination-based variance bounds, and a label-outlier simulation rather than a deep-network size sweep. The robust variance result is derived from bounds on the baseline predictive variance.
record.method_sensitivity: The label-contamination level η changes the reported peak magnitude; the authors say its location remains stable. The variance upper bound also depends on the truncation interval.

fits_no_version.finding: Contamination-induced lower and upper predictive-variance envelopes keep the double-descent peak location of the baseline Bayesian random-feature predictive variance. This holds by construction, as positive rescalings, assuming the baseline already shows double descent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Robust (credal) Bayesian predictive variance bounds inherit the baseline double-descent peak location.

record.problems: The test-MSE and variance curves are presented as figures without tabulated values or reported error bars. The formal peak-preservation result assumes that baseline predictive variance already exhibits double descent; the upper variance bound uses a truncation approximation.

untested.parts: Only random-feature regression is tested, with no other model classes and no comparison against the classical U-curve.
Untested: whether optimally tuned ridge removes the peak, and whether there are multiple or triple peaks. Only an outlier-type label contamination is tested, not standard label noise at varying σ.

record.verdict_notes: Results are figure-only with no numbers or error bars, and σ, A, n/d and the number of seeds are not stated. Rows R6–R8 were reclassified because the envelopes are derived, not observed. The study cites Belkin et al. 2019 (an original source) but is not itself an original.

versions.untested_parts: The experiments concern random-feature regression, not deep networks.
No sweep over training epochs or training time.
No sweep over the number of training samples near the interpolation threshold.
Tests a feature-count sweep in random-feature regression only, not a range of model classes or capacity measures.
Does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across axes.
Tests variance behavior and label-contamination effects on the peak. Does not test multiple or triple peaks, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak.
Does not re-express complexity using an effective parameter count or test whether that changes the curve to an ordinary U-shape.

relationships.condition: Random-feature regression (ridgeless for Figure 2), sweeping N/d at fixed n/d, η = 0 to 0.1
relationships.reason: Test error falls, peaks sharply near N = n, then falls again in a non-deep model class (R1, R2, R3, R4, R5).
relationships.display_finding: Test error initially fell, peaked sharply near N = n, and then fell again.

relationships.condition: Random-feature regression; bias-variance decomposition and label-outlier contamination η ∈ {0.02, 0.05, 0.1}
relationships.reason: The peak is entirely variance-driven with smooth bias (R1), and peak height grows with the outlier fraction while its location stays stable (R3, R4, R5).
relationships.display_finding: Bias remained smooth while variance produced the entire peak, whose height increased across outlier fractions 0.02, 0.05, and 0.1 without shifting location.
